title: $24 an Hour Is How Much a Year? (2026)
metaDescription: $24/hour is $49,920 a year at 40 hrs/week — $4,160 monthly, $1,920.00 biweekly. See overtime pay tables and a 2026 federal take-home estimate.

hero.lede: Full time at 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year (2,080 hours). Below: every pay-period equivalent, overtime tables at time-and-a-half, and a 2026 federal-only take-home estimate.

shortAnswer.heading: How much is $24 an hour per year?
shortAnswer.html: $24 an hour is $49,920 a year at 40 hours a week for 52 weeks (2,080 hours). That's $960.00 a week, $1,920.00 biweekly, and $4,160.00 a month gross. After estimated federal income tax and FICA, a single filer keeps about $42,291 — and steady overtime at $36.00/hour raises the total fast.

sections.title: What $24/hour adds up to per period.
sections.note: Gross (pre-tax) figures assuming paid hours every week of the year. Unpaid time off reduces them proportionally.

sections.title: $24 an hour in 2026, in plain numbers.
paragraphs: At $24 an hour, a full-time year — 40 hours a week for 52 weeks, with no unpaid time off — grosses $49,920. That's $960.00 a week, $1,920.00 per biweekly paycheck, and about $4,160.00 a month before taxes.

Measured against the middle of the U.S. labor market, $24/hour is about 23% below the U.S. median full-time wage — the BLS median works out to about $31.28/hour ($1,251/week, BLS, Q2 2026). The big lever for hourly earners is overtime: every OT hour pays $36.00 at time-and-a-half.

sections.title: Overtime at $36.00/hour changes the math quickly.
sections.note: Overtime rows assume time-and-a-half (1.5 × $24 = $36.00) on hours past 40, every week of the year — the FLSA baseline for non-exempt workers.

sections.title: From $49,920 gross to take-home.
sections.note: Single filer, standard deduction, no state/local income tax, credits, or pre-tax benefits. Actual checks vary.

sections.title: What a single filer actually keeps.
paragraphs: Federally, this wage puts a single filer in the 12% marginal bracket for 2026: $49,920 gross less the $16,100 standard deduction is $33,820 taxable, generating $3,810 of income tax (7.6% effective). Add $3,819 of FICA and estimated take-home is $42,291/year, or $3,524.23/month.

faq.q: How much is $24 an hour per year?
faq.a: $24 an hour is $49,920 a year at full time — 40 hours a week for 52 weeks (2,080 hours). At 30 hours a week it comes to $37,440, and with 10 hours of weekly overtime it reaches about $68,640.

faq.q: How much is $24 an hour biweekly?
faq.a: A standard 80-hour biweekly period at $24/hour grosses $1,920.00. After estimated federal income tax and FICA for a single filer, roughly $1,626.57 remains per check, before state taxes.

faq.q: How much is $24 an hour after taxes?
faq.a: On $49,920 of annual wages, a single filer taking the 2026 standard deduction pays about $3,810 of federal income tax plus $3,819 of FICA, keeping roughly $42,291 a year — about $20.33 per hour worked. State and local taxes reduce this further where they apply.

faq.q: How much is $24 an hour with overtime?
faq.a: Overtime pays time-and-a-half: $36.00 per hour past 40 in a week. A steady 50-hour week earns $1,320.00 weekly — $68,640 a year, $18,720 more than the straight 40-hour year.

faq.q: Is $24 an hour a good wage in 2026?
faq.a: $24/hour annualizes to $49,920, which is about 23% below the U.S. median full-time wage — the BLS median for full-time workers is $1,251/week (about $31.28/hour, BLS, Q2 2026). Local cost of living, benefits, and schedule stability matter as much as the rate itself.

methodology: Annualization is straight arithmetic: $24 × 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks) = $49,920, with daily/weekly/biweekly/monthly rows derived the same way. No unpaid leave is assumed.
Overtime rows use the FLSA non-exempt baseline of 1.5× base pay ($36.00/hour) on hours over 40 per week, sustained all 52 weeks.
The take-home estimate uses 2026 federal brackets for a single filer with the $16,100 standard deduction plus employee FICA (7.65%). It excludes state/local tax, credits, and pre-tax benefits.
Median-wage comparison: BLS median usual weekly earnings, full-time workers, $1,251/week (BLS, Q2 2026).
